The document provides guidelines for conducting HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending antenatal clinics (ANC) using routine program data. This effort is a collaboration between WHO, UNAIDS, and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The guidelines are based on country experiences and expert reviews. The development of the document was coordinated by WHO and CDC, with significant technical input from experts at WHO, CDC, Imperial College London, and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, among others. The findings and recommendations represent the views of WHO and UNAIDS and may not reflect the official position of the CDC. Funding for this work was provided by the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), UNAIDS, and WHO. The purpose of this guidance document is to assist national HIV surveillance program staff in monitoring trends in HIV epidemics. It outlines how routine data from prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs can be used for HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC. The guidelines assume that programs have already assessed the readiness of routine data for surveillance purposes, as described in WHO’s 2013 guidelines on PMTCT data utility for HIV sentinel surveillance. The technical guidance covers various aspects of surveillance, including design, site selection, sample size calculation, data collection, analysis, interpretation, monitoring, and dissemination of results. It is informed by input from surveillance experts and lessons learned from the field. Countries are encouraged to adapt the guidance as needed. HIV surveillance among pregnant women is critical for understanding the epidemic and planning interventions. Over the past two decades, ANC-based HIV surveillance has provided valuable insights into the burden and trends of HIV prevalence. Historically, this surveillance relied on unlinked anonymous testing (UAT). While limitations and biases exist, ANC-based surveillance remains a useful proxy for HIV prevalence trends in the general female population. Complementary data sources, such as household surveys and key population surveys, enhance the understanding of the epidemic’s direction, subnational variations, and localized high-burden areas. Data from ANC-based HIV surveillance also contribute to statistical models estimating national and subnational HIV burden and incidence. Routine program data for HIV surveillance have improved significantly in recent years, with expanded access to diagnostic testing, higher PMTCT and antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage, and the adoption of lifelong ART for HIV-positive pregnant women (Option B+). In 2014, approximately 50% of pregnant women in lowand middle-income countries underwent HIV testing and received their results, and 73% of HIV-positive pregnant women received ART to prevent mother-to-child transmission. As programs expand, routine data increasingly capture demographic, HIV, and syphilis information previously obtained through UAT-based surveillance. This approach requires fewer resources, supports system sustainability, and allows for broader surveillance coverage. Effective HIV surveillance among pregnant women relies on collaboration with multiple programs, including those not directly related to surveillance. Routine data collection, testing strategies, and quality assurance are typically managed by maternal and child health (MCH) or PMTCT programs, while data systems are overseen by informatics units or health partners. Surveillance efforts should engage programmatic partners early and use findings to strengthen routine data quality and service delivery. Ethical considerations are paramount in HIV surveillance. All activities must adhere to principles of respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. Protocols should be reviewed and approved by ethical boards, and informed consent is not required for surveillance based on routine data. Surveillance staff must be trained in data security and confidentiality procedures. The surveillance design should provide reliable epidemiological data while being resource-efficient. A census approach, using either individual-level or aggregate data, is preferred for its comprehensive coverage and ability to support detailed analyses. However, many countries may not yet be ready for a census approach due to limited electronic medical record (EMR) systems or data quality challenges. Sentinel surveillance remains a viable alternative in such cases. Variables for surveillance should be carefully selected to support epidemiological analysis and public health action. Core variables include visit date, age, HIV testing status, and ART status. Non-core variables, such as gravidity, parity, marital status, and educational level, may also be collected if available and relevant. Syphilis surveillance among pregnant women is often integrated with HIV surveillance due to shared transmission pathways and program platforms. Routine syphilis testing and treatment during pregnancy are essential for preventing adverse outcomes and are supported by WHO and national policies. Dual elimination initiatives for mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis have been launched in several regions. Surveillance of syphilis should be incorporated into HIV surveillance efforts, with core indicators including testing coverage, seropositivity, and treatment rates. In summary, this guidance document provides a comprehensive framework for conducting HIV surveillance among pregnant women using routine program data. It emphasizes ethical principles, collaboration, and the use of high-quality data to inform public health action.
